# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Monitor for signs of asthma exacerbation, including increased wheezing, changes in oxygen saturation, and worsening symptoms during flour handling. Monitor for adherence to current medication regimen.
Investigate the patient's work environment to assess exposure to occupational triggers such as flour. Consider pulmonary function tests (PFTs) to evaluate asthma control and severity.
Refer the patient to a respiratory specialist or occupational health physician for further evaluation of occupational asthma and management strategies.

Recommend the patient to avoid exposure to flour and other occupational triggers at work. Provide education on asthma triggers, inhaler technique, and the importance of adherence to prescribed medication.
Schedule a follow-up appointment in one week to reassess asthma control, review inhaler technique, and evaluate any changes in symptoms or exposure to triggers.

Review the patient's current medication regimen, including the use of budesonide/formoterol inhaler. Ensure that the patient understands the correct technique for inhaler use and the importance of regular use.
Clarify the patient's current medication use, including the frequency and adherence to the budesonide/formoterol inhaler. Clarify any uncertainties regarding allergy status.

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

Refer the patient to a general practitioner for a comprehensive asthma management review and inhaler technique training. The patient's daughter may assist in this process.

Encourage the patient to maintain a healthy lifestyle, including regular physical activity and a balanced diet, to support overall respiratory and joint health. Avoid exposure to known triggers that may exacerbate asthma symptoms.

Schedule a follow-up appointment with the general practitioner to assess the patient's asthma control and inhaler technique. This should occur within the next 4-12 weeks to evaluate the effectiveness of the current management plan.

Review the patient's current medication regimen, including the use of beclometasone and salbutamol inhalers. Ensure that the patient is aware of the correct technique for using these medications and that there are no known allergies or interactions.
Clarify the patient's allergy status and any potential interactions with current medications. This is important for ensuring safe and effective treatment.
Clarify the patient's prescription schedules and ensure that there is a clear understanding of when and how to use the inhalers. This will help prevent missed doses and improve symptom control.
Clarify the patient's observed device use and any challenges they may be experiencing with inhaler administration. This will help identify any areas for improvement in technique or support.

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |

* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)

* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE
ICD-10-J44.9

**WHEN TO SUSPECT?**
*   Symptoms – chronic cough, progressively worsening breathlessness
*   Risk factors – tobacco smoking, use of solid fuels for cooking, occupational exposures, Age - >35 years
*   Supportive features: Barrel shaped chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds and rhonchi on chest auscultation, forced expiratory time > 6 seconds, features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
*   No other alternative explanation for these symptoms

**TRY AND RULE OUT**
*   Other obstructive airway disorders – Refer Asthma STW (Table 1) for features that favor COPD over asthma
*   Pulmonary tuberculosis – sputum AFB examination in case of cough ( >2 weeks)
*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

**DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**
*   Airway obstruction should be documented on spirometry on all patients provisionally diagnosed as having COPD – refer if necessary. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/ FVC <0.70 defines airflow obstruction
*   Assess severity based on spirometry, severity of dyspnea (mMRC scale, Table 1), exacerbation frequency and presence of complications (see Table 2)

**TREATMENT**
*   Advice smoking cessation and counsel for other risk factors
*   Inhaled drugs are the mainstay
*   Treatment based on severity assessment (See adjacent figure)
*   Follow up: Mild to moderate disease - 3 to 6 months; Severe disease - 1-3 months
*   Ensure compliance and proper inhaler technique at each visit.
*   If uncontrolled/ complications develop, refer to higher center

**Disease progression flowchart:**
*   Disease progression -> Mild COPD
*   Disease progression -> Moderate COPD
*   Disease progression -> Severe COPD
*   Mild COPD -> Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Moderate COPD -> Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Severe COPD -> Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Mild branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Moderate branch) -> Add low dose methylxanthines
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Severe branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis

**DISEASE EXACERBATION**
**Three cardinal symptoms:**
*   Increase in dyspnea
*   Increase in sputum volume and/or
*   Increase in sputum purulence

**Classify As:**
*   Mild Exacerbation
*   Severe Exacerbation

**Features Of Severe Exacerbation:**
*   Cyanosis
*   Respiratory rate >30/ min
*   Heart rate >110/min
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   SpO2 <90%
*   Paradoxical respiratory movements
*   Altered sensorium
*   Asterixis
*   Presence of severe co-morbid conditions (e.g. heart failure, arrhythmia)

**MILD EXACERBATION**
*   Increase dose and/ or frequency of levosalbutamol and/ or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg), repeated as needed at 20-minute interval
*   Amoxycillin 500 mg TDS/ Azithromycin 500 mg OD/ Doxycycline 100 mg OD (BD on day 1) X 5 Days
*   Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily X 5 days

**SEVERE EXACERBATION**
*   Treatment as under Mild Exacerbation
*   + Supplement oxygen with target spO2 of 92% (if spO2 monitoring available)

**TABLE 1. GRADING OF BREATHLESSNESS USING MODIFIED MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL (MMRC) SCALE.**

| GRADE | DESCRIPTION OF BREATHLESSNESS |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | I only get breathless with strenuous exercise. |
| 1 | I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill. |
| 2 | On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace. |
| 3 | I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground. |
| 4 | I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing. |

**TABLE 2. SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION FOR COPD**

| SEVERITY | POSTBRONCHODILATOR FEV1 (% PREDICTED) | DYSPNEA (MMRC GRADE) | EXACERBATIONS IN LAST ONE YEAR | COMPLICATIONS* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MILD | $\geq$ 80 | <2 | <2 | NO |
| MODERATE | 50-79 | $\geq$ 2 | <2 | NO |
| SEVERE | <50 | $\geq$ 2 | $\geq$ 2 | YES |

The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
*Complications include respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

**RED FLAG SIGNS FOR PEOPLE HAVING EXCERBATION**
*   Altered sensorium
*   spO2 <88% despite therapy
*   Heart rate >110 bpm
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   High risk comorbid conditions (arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure)

**Refer to higher centre for further management, and ensure continued supplemental oxygen and nebulization during transfer**

**SCHEDULE FOLLOW UP VISIT ONE WEEK AFTER DISCHARGE**

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Monitor the patient's respiratory status, including oxygen saturation, breathlessness, and any new or worsening symptoms. Pay particular attention to signs of exacerbation such as increased dyspnea, changes in sputum volume or purulence, and any new or worsening fatigue.

Investigate the cause of the weight loss and poor appetite. Consider evaluating for underlying conditions such as malignancy, thyroid dysfunction, or malabsorption. A dietary assessment should be conducted to evaluate nutritional status and identify potential dietary deficiencies.

Refer the patient to a general practitioner for further evaluation of the weight loss and fatigue. This should include a comprehensive review of the patient's medical history, dietary habits, and any potential contributing factors.

Encourage the patient to maintain a balanced diet and adequate caloric intake to address the weight loss. Provide support for cooking and meal preparation, especially given the patient's reported fatigue and difficulty with cooking. Consider involving a dietitian for personalized dietary advice.

Schedule a follow-up visit with the general practitioner to reassess the patient's weight, appetite, and overall health status. This should include a review of any new or worsening symptoms and a reassessment of the patient's nutritional status.

Review the patient's current medication regimen, including the use of tiotropium inhaler. Ensure that the patient is using the inhaler correctly and that there are no adverse effects contributing to the weight loss or fatigue. Consider the possibility of medication-related side effects.

Clarify the patient's height and allergy status, as these are missing from the medical record. This information is important for a comprehensive assessment of the patient's health and for determining appropriate interventions.

Clarify the patient's history of weight loss and any previous investigations related to the weight loss. This will help in understanding the context of the current weight loss and in determining the appropriate management plan.

1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE
ICD-10-J44.9

**WHEN TO SUSPECT?**
*   Symptoms – chronic cough, progressively worsening breathlessness
*   Risk factors – tobacco smoking, use of solid fuels for cooking, occupational exposures, Age - >35 years
*   Supportive features: Barrel shaped chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds and rhonchi on chest auscultation, forced expiratory time > 6 seconds, features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
*   No other alternative explanation for these symptoms

**TRY AND RULE OUT**
*   Other obstructive airway disorders – Refer Asthma STW (Table 1) for features that favor COPD over asthma
*   Pulmonary tuberculosis – sputum AFB examination in case of cough ( >2 weeks)
*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

**DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**
*   Airway obstruction should be documented on spirometry on all patients provisionally diagnosed as having COPD – refer if necessary. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/ FVC <0.70 defines airflow obstruction
*   Assess severity based on spirometry, severity of dyspnea (mMRC scale, Table 1), exacerbation frequency and presence of complications (see Table 2)

**TREATMENT**
*   Advice smoking cessation and counsel for other risk factors
*   Inhaled drugs are the mainstay
*   Treatment based on severity assessment (See adjacent figure)
*   Follow up: Mild to moderate disease - 3 to 6 months; Severe disease - 1-3 months
*   Ensure compliance and proper inhaler technique at each visit.
*   If uncontrolled/ complications develop, refer to higher center

**Disease progression flowchart:**
*   Disease progression -> Mild COPD
*   Disease progression -> Moderate COPD
*   Disease progression -> Severe COPD
*   Mild COPD -> Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Moderate COPD -> Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Severe COPD -> Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Mild branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Moderate branch) -> Add low dose methylxanthines
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Severe branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis

**DISEASE EXACERBATION**
**Three cardinal symptoms:**
*   Increase in dyspnea
*   Increase in sputum volume and/or
*   Increase in sputum purulence

**Classify As:**
*   Mild Exacerbation
*   Severe Exacerbation

**Features Of Severe Exacerbation:**
*   Cyanosis
*   Respiratory rate >30/ min
*   Heart rate >110/min
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   SpO2 <90%
*   Paradoxical respiratory movements
*   Altered sensorium
*   Asterixis
*   Presence of severe co-morbid conditions (e.g. heart failure, arrhythmia)

**MILD EXACERBATION**
*   Increase dose and/ or frequency of levosalbutamol and/ or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg), repeated as needed at 20-minute interval
*   Amoxycillin 500 mg TDS/ Azithromycin 500 mg OD/ Doxycycline 100 mg OD (BD on day 1) X 5 Days
*   Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily X 5 days

**SEVERE EXACERBATION**
*   Treatment as under Mild Exacerbation
*   + Supplement oxygen with target spO2 of 92% (if spO2 monitoring available)

**TABLE 1. GRADING OF BREATHLESSNESS USING MODIFIED MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL (MMRC) SCALE.**

| GRADE | DESCRIPTION OF BREATHLESSNESS |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | I only get breathless with strenuous exercise. |
| 1 | I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill. |
| 2 | On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace. |
| 3 | I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground. |
| 4 | I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing. |

**TABLE 2. SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION FOR COPD**

| SEVERITY | POSTBRONCHODILATOR FEV1 (% PREDICTED) | DYSPNEA (MMRC GRADE) | EXACERBATIONS IN LAST ONE YEAR | COMPLICATIONS* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MILD | $\geq$ 80 | <2 | <2 | NO |
| MODERATE | 50-79 | $\geq$ 2 | <2 | NO |
| SEVERE | <50 | $\geq$ 2 | $\geq$ 2 | YES |

The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
*Complications include respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

**RED FLAG SIGNS FOR PEOPLE HAVING EXCERBATION**
*   Altered sensorium
*   spO2 <88% despite therapy
*   Heart rate >110 bpm
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   High risk comorbid conditions (arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure)

**Refer to higher centre for further management, and ensure continued supplemental oxygen and nebulization during transfer**

**SCHEDULE FOLLOW UP VISIT ONE WEEK AFTER DISCHARGE**

2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

### MANAGEMENT ALGORITHM

Sign/ symptoms suggestive of AF -> Confirm by 12 channel rhythm strip -> Hemodynamic Instability

* Hemodynamic Instability -> **Yes** -> Drug version
    * Drug version -> **Successful** -> Continue drug
    * Drug version -> **No** -> DC version
* Hemodynamic Instability -> **No** -> Very rapid HR >130/ min
    * Very rapid HR >130/ min -> **Yes** -> CHF
        * CHF -> **Yes** -> HR control Aim <110/min
            * HR control Aim <110/min -> **Careful BB/Dig Amiodarone**
            * HR control Aim <110/min -> **HR > 110/ min** -> Consider DC version
        * CHF -> **No** -> BB or Ca Block or combine
    * Very rapid HR >130/ min -> **No** -> Symptomatic
        * Symptomatic -> **Yes** -> Clinical Follow-up
        * Symptomatic -> **No** -> Clinical Follow-up

---

**Anti-coagulants in all Except**
* Reversible
* Score <1 (men) ; <2 (women)

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### LOOK FOR IMMEDIATE INTERVENTION INDICATORS:
* Systolic BP 90 mmHg, HR > 150 or <50/min
* Ongoing Angina
* CHF or TIA or stroke
* Major bleed on Oral Anti-coagulants

| STROKE RISK SCORE | SCORE |
| :--- | :--- |
| **CHA$_{DS}$-VASC$_{2}$** | |
| - Congestive heart failure/LV dysfunction | 1 |
| - Hypertension | 1 |
| - Aged > 75 years | 2 |
| - Diabetes mellitus | 1 |
| - Stroke/ TIA/ TE | 2 |
| - Vascular disease [prior MI, PAD or aortic plaque] | 1 |
| - Aged 65-74 years | 1 |
| - Sex category [i.e. female gender] | 1 |
| **Maximum Score** | **9** |

OAC if score >1 in men and >2 in women

| BLEEDING RISK SCORE | SCORE |
| :--- | :--- |
| **HAS-BLED** | |
| - Hypertension i.e. uncontrolled BP | 1 |
| - Abnormal renal/ liver function | 1 or 2 |
| - Stroke | 1 |
| - Bleeding tendency or predisposition | 1 |
| - Labile INR | 1 |
| - Age (e.g. >65) | 1 |
| - Drugs (e.g. concomitant aspirin or NSAIDs or alcohol | 1 |
| **Maximum Score** | **9** |

Bleeding Risk High in score >3

---

**CHOICE OF ANTI-COAGULATION:**
* Vitamin K antagonist
    * Aim for INR 2-3
* Assess risk of bleeding
* Take measures to reduce/ modify risk of bleeding
* Dietary modification & regular monitoring

**MEASURES TO REDUCE HIGH BLEEDING RISK:**
* Control SBP to less than 140 mmHg
* Avoid dietary indiscretions
* Avoid concomitant aspirin, anti platelets, NSAIDs
* Avoid alcohol
* Correct anemia

### MANAGEMENT
**AT PHC/ CHC:**
* Detailed clinical evaluation
* Basic investigations
* Careful ECG evaluation
* Start OAC if indicated (based on Stroke risk)
* Start Metoprolol if HR >110/ min & no evidence of CHF
* Refer if indicators for early intervention

**AT DISTRICT HOSPITAL:**
* Admit if indicators of early interventions
* Immediate cardioversion after heparinization, if hemodynamic instability
* Manage precipitating factors if any
* Assess stroke, bleeding risk & coagulation parameters
* Detailed echocardiogram
* Start OAC, maintain INR around 2-3
* Control HR by single drug or combination of BB & Ca Blocker
* Refer HR uncontrolled or CHF or angina

**AT TERTIARY CENTRE:**
* Re-assess clinical status, adequacy of AC
* Consider need of NOAC
* Optimise management of underlying cardiac disease
* Stress life style and AF risk factor modification
* Assess need for rhythm control and discuss pros & cons
* Consider RFA in select patient

evidence_sources.original_text:
## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

related_icmr_context.original_text:
# TREATMENT

### GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Avoidance of allergens and irritant materials
• Daily bath with mild soap, keep nails short, avoid scratching
• Moisturizer are cornerstone in the management of eczema; to be applied immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp and apply multiple times during the day
• Antihistamines for (eg. levocetirizine) for control of pruritus
• Topical corticosteroids (TCS) mild – Over face/ flexures genitals. Mid potent TCS over palms, soles and lichenified lesions
• Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs)- Face/ flexures genitals and/or as maintenance treatment
• If secondary infection (pain, pus discharge, yellow crust)- Treat with topical/ oral antibiotic as needed

### SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT
**Primary/Secondary Level**
• Treatment of active eczema: Daily use of TCS of appropriate strength until completely clear ± antihistamine (for sedative/antipruritic effects) ± oral antibiotic course (if superinfection) - (refer to STW on rational use of topical therapy)
• Maintenance treatment for area where lesions are more resistant to treatment or there is propensity for relapse, like flexural skin- Intermittent use of mid-potency TCS (e.g. 2-3 days/week) and/or TCI (e.g. 3–5 days/week)

**Tertiary Level**
• Severe disease in addition to above may require phototherapy or systemic treatment (Short course of oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine etc.)

***

**AVOIDANCE OF PROVOKING AGENTS, MOISTURIZERS AND EARLY TREATMENT ARE THE AIM OF ECZEMA MANAGEMENT**

# TREATMENT

### GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Avoidance of allergens and irritant materials
• Daily bath with mild soap, keep nails short, avoid scratching
• Moisturizer are cornerstone in the management of eczema; to be applied immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp and apply multiple times during the day
• Antihistamines for (eg. levocetirizine) for control of pruritus
• Topical corticosteroids (TCS) mild – Over face/ flexures genitals. Mid potent TCS over palms, soles and lichenified lesions
• Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs)- Face/ flexures genitals and/or as maintenance treatment
• If secondary infection (pain, pus discharge, yellow crust)- Treat with topical/ oral antibiotic as needed

### SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT
**Primary/Secondary Level**
• Treatment of active eczema: Daily use of TCS of appropriate strength until completely clear ± antihistamine (for sedative/antipruritic effects) ± oral antibiotic course (if superinfection) - (refer to STW on rational use of topical therapy)
• Maintenance treatment for area where lesions are more resistant to treatment or there is propensity for relapse, like flexural skin- Intermittent use of mid-potency TCS (e.g. 2-3 days/week) and/or TCI (e.g. 3–5 days/week)

**Tertiary Level**
• Severe disease in addition to above may require phototherapy or systemic treatment (Short course of oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine etc.)

***

**AVOIDANCE OF PROVOKING AGENTS, MOISTURIZERS AND EARLY TREATMENT ARE THE AIM OF ECZEMA MANAGEMENT**

related_icmr_context.text:
# TREATMENT

### GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Avoidance of allergens and irritant materials
• Daily bath with mild soap, keep nails short, avoid scratching
• Moisturizer are cornerstone in the management of eczema; to be applied immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp and apply multiple times during the day
• Antihistamines for (eg. levocetirizine) for control of pruritus
• Topical corticosteroids (TCS) mild – Over face/ flexures genitals. Mid potent TCS over palms, soles and lichenified lesions
• Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs)- Face/ flexures genitals and/or as maintenance treatment
• If secondary infection (pain, pus discharge, yellow crust)- Treat with topical/ oral antibiotic as needed

### SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT
**Primary/Secondary Level**
• Treatment of active eczema: Daily use of TCS of appropriate strength until completely clear ± antihistamine (for sedative/antipruritic effects) ± oral antibiotic course (if superinfection) - (refer to STW on rational use of topical therapy)
• Maintenance treatment for area where lesions are more resistant to treatment or there is propensity for relapse, like flexural skin- Intermittent use of mid-potency TCS (e.g. 2-3 days/week) and/or TCI (e.g. 3–5 days/week)

**Tertiary Level**
• Severe disease in addition to above may require phototherapy or systemic treatment (Short course of oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine etc.)

***

**AVOIDANCE OF PROVOKING AGENTS, MOISTURIZERS AND EARLY TREATMENT ARE THE AIM OF ECZEMA MANAGEMENT**

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of HEADACHE ICD-10-G43-44

**TREATMENT FLOWCHART**
**LEGEND/ INDEX/ KEY**
* Type of Headache (Green)
* Management at PHC (Yellow)
* Management at district hospital (Dark teal)

**Flowchart Pathways:**
* CONTINUOUS HEADACHES (Progressive headache of acute or subacute onset persisting more than 1 week. Possibilities: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis, Intra Cranial Space Occupying Lesion, Meningitis, Brain abscess) -> Referred to higher centre -> [CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram, Lumbar puncture, Refer to tertiary care centre]
* CHRONIC TENSION HEADACHE (Continuous bilateral headache for many years with significant insomnia and psychosomatic complaints.) -> Start Amitriptyline (10mg HS) and advice on lifestyle -> Brain imaging if atypical features exist
* MIGRAINE (Side alternating, associated visual aura, photo-phono phobia, nausea, relieved by sleep or analgesics) -> [Frequency > 2 /month - Start prophylaxis trial for 2 months: Propranolol 40 mg OD, Flunarizine 10 mg OD; Acute management: Analgesics (Paracetamol 650 mg, or Indomethacin 50 mg) and Antiemetics (Prochlorperazine 10mg). Lifestyle changes: Good sleep at least 6 hrs, food habit modification, avoiding triggers of migraine.] -> Brain imaging if there are atypical symptoms
* ATYPICAL MIGRAINE (Hemiplegia, visual impairment, vertigo) -> Analgesics for pain, Refer to higher centre with imaging facility -> [CT/ MRI with MR angiogram or CT angiogram if required, Migraine prophylaxis after ruling out stroke and other diseases]
* TRIGEMINAL AUTONOMIC CEPHALGIAS (Rapid onset peri orbital and temporal pain with autonomic features) -> Indomethacin (25mg TID) for 7 days -> Refer to tertiary care centre
* CLUSTER HEADACHE, PAROXYSMAL HEMICRANIAS, SHORT LASTING UNILATERAL NEURALGIFORM PAIN WITH CONJUNCTIVAL INJECTION AND TEARING SYNDROME (SUNCT) -> Refer to tertiary care centre -> Refer to tertiary care centre

**RED FLAG SIGNS**
* First or worst headache of the patient's life
* Focal neurologic signs (not typical aura)
* Severe headache awakening from sleep
* Headache with fever, change in personality, mental status, level of consciousness
* Fever, neck stiffness or meningism
* New onset of severe headache in pregnancy or postpartum or while on hormone treatment
* Rapid onset with strenuous exercise
* Sudden onset (maximal intensity occurs within seconds to minutes, thunderclap headache)
* New headache type in a patient with malignancy or immunosuppression

**REASONS FOR REFERRAL**
* Non responding headaches
* Headaches with danger signs should be immediately referred and investigated for potentially dangerous conditions

**TREATMENT OF MAJOR CATASTROPHIC HEADACHES AT TERTIARY CENTRE**
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE -> Angiogram, clipping/ coiling of aneurysm (to prevent rebleed)
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE -> Stroke unit admission and neurosurgery for cortical hemorrhages or large hemorrhage with herniation
* Progressive headache -> MR venogram -> CEREBRAL VENOUS THROMBOSIS -> Intravenous UFH / subcutaneous heparin/LMWH
* Headache with fever, personality change, altered sensorium, neck stiffness -> CT scan followed by CSF study -> MENINGIOENCEPHALITIS -> Antibiotics/ antivirals
* Progressive headache with seizure or focal deficit -> CT/MRI with contrast -> BRAIN TUMORS -> Surgery, radiation, chemotherapy

**INDICATIONS FOR ADMISSION**
* Patient with unrelenting headache
* Immunosuppressed patients with continuous headache,
* First ever headache with worsening intensity,
* Progressive headache with other systemic disease
* Severe symptomatic primary headache disorders

**CRITERIA FOR DISCHARGE**
* Primary headache disorders- symptomatically improved severe episode of headache due to primary headache disorder can be discharged
* Secondary headache disorders- secondary headache disorders with essential work up, diagnosis and treatment as per individual case can be discharged

**FOLLOW UP OF HEADACHE PATIENTS**
| CAUSES OF HEADACHE | TREATMENT OF HEADACHE |
| :--- | :--- |
| Intra cerebral hemorrhage | Good control of blood pressure |
| Seizures | Antiepileptic medications |
| Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis | Follow up of anticoagulation |
| Migraine | Give prophylaxis for adequate duration of time and taper after remission |

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Schedule a same-day general practitioner visit for evaluation of headache pattern changes.

Recommend maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, particularly addressing the impact of alternating shifts on sleep quality. Encourage the patient to prioritize 7-9 hours of sleep per night and consider strategies to improve sleep hygiene.
Monitor the frequency, intensity, and duration of headaches. Note any changes in pattern, including the presence of new symptoms such as neurological deficits, fever, or changes in mental status.
Schedule a follow-up visit in 2 weeks to reassess headache frequency and response to lifestyle modifications. If symptoms persist or worsen, consider further evaluation.

Review the patient's medication history for any potential interactions or contraindications. Since no current medications are reported, ensure that the patient is not using any over-the-counter medications that may contribute to headache frequency.
Clarify the patient's understanding of the headache pattern and the importance of reporting any changes. Ensure the patient is aware of the red flag signs that require immediate medical attention.

Consider imaging or other diagnostic tests if there are any atypical features or if the headache pattern changes significantly. This may include MRI or CT scans if there are concerns about secondary causes.

* First or worst headache of the patient's life
* Focal neurologic signs (not typical aura)
* Severe headache awakening from sleep
* Headache with fever, change in personality, mental status, level of consciousness
* Fever, neck stiffness or meningism
* New onset of severe headache in pregnancy or postpartum or while on hormone treatment
* Rapid onset with strenuous exercise
* Sudden onset (maximal intensity occurs within seconds to minutes, thunderclap headache)
* New headache type in a patient with malignancy or immunosuppression

**REASONS FOR REFERRAL**
* Non responding headaches
* Headaches with danger signs should be immediately referred and investigated for potentially dangerous conditions

**TREATMENT OF MAJOR CATASTROPHIC HEADACHES AT TERTIARY CENTRE**

* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE -> Stroke unit admission and neurosurgery for cortical hemorrhages or large hemorrhage with herniation
* Progressive headache -> MR venogram -> CEREBRAL VENOUS THROMBOSIS -> Intravenous UFH / subcutaneous heparin/LMWH
* Headache with fever, personality change, altered sensorium, neck stiffness -> CT scan followed by CSF study -> MENINGIOENCEPHALITIS -> Antibiotics/ antivirals
* Progressive headache with seizure or focal deficit -> CT/MRI with contrast -> BRAIN TUMORS -> Surgery, radiation, chemotherapy

**INDICATIONS FOR ADMISSION**
* Patient with unrelenting headache
* Immunosuppressed patients with continuous headache,
* First ever headache with worsening intensity,
* Progressive headache with other systemic disease
* Severe symptomatic primary headache disorders

**CRITERIA FOR DISCHARGE**
* Primary headache disorders- symptomatically improved severe episode of headache due to primary headache disorder can be discharged
* Secondary headache disorders- secondary headache disorders with essential work up, diagnosis and treatment as per individual case can be discharged

**FOLLOW UP OF HEADACHE PATIENTS**
| CAUSES OF HEADACHE | TREATMENT OF HEADACHE |
| :--- | :--- |
| Intra cerebral hemorrhage | Good control of blood pressure |
| Seizures | Antiepileptic medications |
| Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis | Follow up of anticoagulation |
| Migraine | Give prophylaxis for adequate duration of time and taper after remission |

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**
